title: Paramesvara Watches Fifty Five Years
subtitle: The Eye That Measured the Sky
era: Drigganita reform and observational astronomy, c. 1393-1443
region: Alathiyur and the Nila valley, Kerala
moral: Truth improves when tradition listens to evidence.

sources.citation: Paramesvara, Drigganita, 1431 CE; Grahanamandana, epoch 1411 CE; Goladipika, 1443 CE
sources.note: Primary texts for the observation-based correction program.

sources.citation: David Pingree, Census of the Exact Sciences in Sanskrit, Series A vol. 4 (1981)
sources.note: Manuscript census listing Paramesvara's large surviving corpus.

sources.citation: K. Ramasubramanian, M.D. Srinivas and M.S. Sriram, Current Science 66:9 (1994); Plofker (2009)
sources.note: Modern account of Kerala model modifications beginning with Paramesvara.

dialogue.text: In fourteenth–fifteenth century Kerala, Vatasseri Parameśvara of Alathiyur watches the heavens for decades, reshaping computation through sight.
On the banks of the Nila in Kerala, the Vatasseri family preserves learning, ritual, and the quiet craft of reckoning the heavens.
From earlier masters he inherits Parahita tables, numbers handed down, meant to serve all: tradition set in verse and digit.
Yet Parameśvara, pupil of Madhava, has learned to suspect numbers that do not meet the sky.
During eclipses in the Nila valley, he does not merely watch in awe. He measures, notes, and remembers.

panels.shot: medium shot over shoulder on manuscripts

dialogue.speaker: vatasseri_paramesvara
dialogue.text: The sky says one thing. The tables say another.
So he begins a long record: eclipses seen in Alathiyur, each bound to numbers that claim to foretell them.
Year after year, eclipse after eclipse, he watches. From about 1411 onward, Alathiyur becomes his observatory.
He teaches that sight itself is a test. Parahita numbers, though revered, must bow if they fail it.
From these efforts grows Grahanamandana, with an epoch set in 1411. Eclipses are no longer just portents, but tests.

panels.shot: medium shot with scrolls and abacus-like counting

dialogue.text: Slowly, he adjusts the constants of the old Parahita system, letting observed eclipses pull the numbers into truer paths.
By 1431, he completes Drigganita—"sight-computation"—a bold title that ties calculation to the act of seeing.

dialogue.speaker: vatasseri_paramesvara
dialogue.text: If computed eclipses match those seen, then our numbers are worthy. Otherwise, we change them.
He also turns to geometry, finding a rule for the circumradius of a cyclic quadrilateral—subtle, precise, and centuries ahead of distant Europe.

panels.shot: wide shot with coastal horizon and star chart

dialogue.text: Kerala’s shores carry merchants and tales to distant lands. His mathematics, quiet on palm leaves, remains rooted here—for now.
By the 1440s, with Goladipika completed, his corpus is large. What joins it is a single thread: the eye ruling the equation.
Across roughly fifty-five years, he lets repeated eclipses grind against tradition, pushing Kerala computation toward a more exact form.
Later scholars will copy and cite his texts. Through them, Parameśvara’s demand is clear: truth must listen to evidence, and even revered tables may change.
